briefs.septic-hip:
Septic Arthritis in a Child: Aspirate, or Treat and Recheck?

Count the Kocher criteria before the needle

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

A septic hip is a surgical emergency: aspirate before antibiotics.

Count the Kocher criteria:

  • Fever over 38.5 °C
  • Refuses to bear weight
  • ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) over 40 mm/h
  • WBC (white blood cell count) over 12,000/mm³
  • CRP (C-reactive protein) over 2.0 mg/dL is often added as a fifth

3 or more: blood culture and ultrasound-guided aspiration. 0 or 1: transient synovitis; NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) and a recheck.

An effusion, and the flexed, abducted, externally rotated hip it causes, occurs in both septic arthritis and transient synovitis; effusions in both hips favor transient synovitis.

Septic fluid (over 50,000 WBC/mm³, neutrophil-predominant) means surgical drainage plus IV antibiotics.

Diagnosis
Kocher criteria Fever – over 38.5 °C · Weight bearing – refuses · ESR – over 40 mm/h · WBC – over 12,000/mm³ · Score – one point each, unweighted
Predictors present: probability of septic arthritis
CountProbabilityAction
0under 0.2%Treat as transient synovitis; recheck
1about 3%Observe with close follow-up
2about 40%Gray zone: 2 alone is below the gate; aspirate if toxic
3about 93%Aspirate
4about 99%Aspirate; surgical urgency
Management and treatment
Management ladder: the painful hip
TierInterventionEscalate when
Kocher 0 to 1Rest and NSAIDs; activity as toleratedFever, refuses to bear weight, or no improvement in 24 to 48 hours
RecheckRepeat CBC, ESR, CRP; re-examine and rescore3 or more criteria, a toxic child with an effusion, or worse
AspirateBlood culture, then ultrasound-guided aspiration, before antibioticsFluid over 50,000 WBC/mm³ or purulent
SepticSurgical drainage plus IV antibioticsTop rung
Before you treat Organisms – S aureus overall; Kingella under 4 years; gonococcus in adolescents; Salmonella in sickle cell disease · Delay – femoral head osteonecrosis and growth arrest · Bone, not joint – fever with point tenderness over the metaphysis, motion preserved: osteomyelitis · On methotrexate – one hot joint out of step with the rest is infection until the fluid says otherwise
Practice
  1. 3-year-old boy with 1 day of right hip pain refuses to bear weight on the right leg cries with any passive movement of the hip No trauma; no recent illness T 39.1 °C · WBC 15,000/mm³ · ESR 62 mm/h → Arthrocentesis → 4 of 4 Kocher criteria (about 99%); draw a blood culture and aspirate before antibiotics
  2. 4-year-old boy limping since a cold 10 days ago today he refuses to bear weight on the left leg holds the left hip flexed and turned outward T 39.2 °C · ESR 78 mm/h · WBC pending → Arthrocentesis before antibiotics → fever, refusal to bear weight and an ESR over 40 are 3 of 4 with the WBC still pending; a recent cold does not make it benign
  3. 7-year-old boy with 2 days of left hip pain will not walk; lies with the hip flexed, abducted and externally rotated screams with gentle passive rotation No point tenderness over the femur T 39.0 °C · WBC 14,000/mm³ · ESR 90 mm/h → Septic arthritis of the hip → Kocher 4 of 4; the position only shows an effusion (it occurs in transient synovitis too); motion this painful is the joint, not the bone
  4. 6-year-old girl with 4 days of a limp after a cold 10 days ago walks, favoring the right leg; well appearing T 37.9 °C · WBC 11,500/mm³ · ESR 18 mm/h · CRP 0.8 mg/dL (normal under 1) · ultrasound: effusions in both hips → Transient synovitis → Kocher 0 of 4; an effusion occurs in both diseases, but effusions in both hips favor transient synovitis (septic arthritis is usually one-sided): NSAIDs and a recheck
  5. 6-year-old girl with 4 days of right knee soreness and a limp began after gymnastics practice right knee: full, painless motion, no swelling or tenderness right hip: internal rotation limited and painful Afebrile · bears weight → Ultrasound of both hips → a normal knee exam sends you to the hip, which refers pain to the knee; ultrasound of both hips looks for effusions
  6. 6-year-old girl with 3 days of a left-sided limp well appearing; walks and bears weight mild pain at the end of hip rotation T 37.4 °C · WBC 8,900/mm³ · ESR 12 mm/h · CRP normal · ultrasound: small effusions in both hips → Arthrocentesis of both hips → Kocher 0 of 4: the needle is for 3 or more; treat and recheck
  7. 4-year-old boy with 2 days of fever and refusal to walk ultrasound-guided hip aspiration: cloudy fluid 80,000 WBC/mm³, 90% neutrophils; Gram stain pending Blood culture drawn before the tap T 39.4 °C · BP 98/60 mm Hg → Surgical drainage plus IV antibiotics → fluid over 50,000 WBC/mm³, neutrophil-predominant: a septic hip is a surgical emergency, and antibiotics alone cannot decompress the joint
  8. 2-year-old boy with sickle cell disease 1 day of fever and refusal to bear weight on the left leg screams when the left hip is moved Ultrasound shows a left hip effusion; aspiration is planned T 39.4 °C · WBC 18,000/mm³ → Salmonella → sickle cell disease adds Salmonella to S aureus; Kingella also fits his age, and gonococcus is the adolescent's
  9. 3-year-old boy with 2 days of fever and refusal to walk hip aspirate: purulent, 95,000 WBC/mm³, mostly neutrophils the operating room is not free until tomorrow Started on IV antibiotics after cultures T 39.2 °C · ESR 70 mm/h → Femoral head osteonecrosis → pus under pressure inside the capsule cuts off blood to the femoral head; delay also risks growth arrest
  10. 4-year-old boy with 4 days of a limp and left thigh pain point tenderness over the distal femoral metaphysis passive hip and knee motion nearly full and only mildly painful Well appearing T 38.6 °C · CRP 6 mg/dL · radiographs normal → Osteomyelitis → fever with point bone tenderness and preserved motion is bone, not joint: MRI; radiographs are normal early
  11. 5-year-old boy treated with ibuprofen for a post-viral limp 4 weeks later he still limps, worse after play hip abduction and internal rotation now limited No fever, night pain or weight loss T 37.0 °C · WBC and ESR normal → Radiographs of both hips → most transient synovitis resolves within 2 weeks; a limp past that needs hip radiographs for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease
  12. 11-year-old girl with polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis on methotrexate wrists, knees and ankles improving 4 days of right shoulder pain, now waking her at night will not move the shoulder T 38.5 °C · synovial fluid 55,000 WBC/mm³, 80% neutrophils → Begin antibiotic therapy → one joint out of step with the rest, with fever and septic fluid on an immunosuppressant: infection, not a flare: antibiotics, then drain the joint; steroid into the joint or more methotrexate would feed it
  13. 4-year-old boy with 1 day of hip pain and a limp cold 10 days ago; no trauma appears well; no bony tenderness hip motion limited by pain Vital signs normal · ultrasound: small right hip effusion · CBC and ESR pending → Ibuprofen and a recheck → afebrile and walking: at most 2 of 4 even if both pending labs return high, and he looks well, so treat and recheck; read the labs when they return; the ultrasound already answered the imaging question, and his pain needs treatment
Pairs with The Limping Child: no hot hip, so match the age and the time. Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis: the adolescent who cannot rotate the hip inward.
Transferable rule

A limp alone is not a reason to aspirate: score Kocher first.

Before ordering another test, name the question it answers that the last one did not.
briefs.limp:
The Limping Child: Sick or Well, Then Age and Time

Is the hip hot, how old is the child, and how long has it been?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Sick first: fever or refusal to bear weight means scoring Kocher and aspirating at 3 or more.

A limp with night pain that wakes the child, weight loss or bruising: CBC (complete blood count) with smear before calling anything benign.

Then match the age:

  • Infant, or a new walker: DDH (developmental dysplasia of the hip)
  • 1 to 3 years: toddler's fracture
  • About 3 to 10: transient synovitis; about 4 to 10: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease
  • 10 to 15: SCFE (slipped capital femoral epiphysis)

Then time it: days point to infection, synovitis or fracture; weeks to months point to Perthes disease, SCFE, JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) or tumor.

Knee pain with a normal knee exam: examine and image the hip.

Diagnosis
Exam tells DDH – Barlow and Ortolani in infants; once walking, a painless limp, a shorter leg and limited abduction · Perthes disease – abduction and internal rotation lost · SCFE – internal rotation lost; the hip rotates outward on flexion · Osgood-Schlatter disease – knee pain with a tender tibial tubercle and a normal hip · Psoas abscess or appendicitis – hip pain on extension (psoas sign) with a normal hip joint
Management and treatment
By diagnosis DDH – Pavlik harness under 6 months; closed reduction and spica cast at 6 to 18 months; untreated, early osteoarthritis · Perthes disease – avoid high-impact activity; NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs); physical therapy · SCFE – no weight bearing; urgent pinning in situ · JIA – slit-lamp exam for uveitis; highest risk when ANA (antinuclear antibody) is positive · Rheumatic fever – ASO (antistreptolysin O) titer and the Jones criteria
Practice
  1. 13-month-old girl, walking for 1 month, with a painless limp born breech asymmetric thigh skin folds left leg shorter; left hip abduction limited Her mother wore a hip harness as an infant Afebrile · no bruising or tenderness → Developmental dysplasia of the hip → breech, female, a family history, a short leg and limited abduction in a new walker: missed DDH; past 4 to 6 months, image with a radiograph
  2. 2-year-old girl with a painless limp since she began walking right leg shorter than the left right hip abduction limited Born at term; no trauma; growth normal Afebrile · knees and ankles normal → Radiograph of the pelvis → missed DDH in a walker: the femoral head has ossified, so a radiograph; ultrasound is for infants under about 4 to 6 months
  3. 2-year-old boy who will not put weight on his right leg began yesterday after a fall at daycare that no one saw tender over the distal right tibia Well appearing Afebrile · CRP normal · hip and knee motion full → Toddler's fracture → a new limp after a minor, unwitnessed fall with tibial tenderness: tibia radiographs for a spiral fracture; corner or bucket-handle fractures suggest abuse
  4. 6-year-old boy with a limp for 2 months, worse after play intermittent groin and knee pain hip abduction and internal rotation limited No fever, trauma or night pain Afebrile · CBC and ESR normal · radiograph: flattened, fragmented femoral head → Legg-Calvé-Perthes → an insidious limp over weeks with normal labs at about 4 to 10 years; early films can be normal, so MRI when they are
  5. 13-year-old boy with 3 weeks of left thigh and knee pain and a limp 95th percentile for height, 50th for weight left hip internal rotation lost; the hip rotates outward when flexed Knee examination normal Afebrile · white cell count normal → Slipped capital femoral epiphysis → lost internal rotation with obligate external rotation at the growth spurt, whatever the build: AP and frog-leg radiographs of both hips
  6. 10-year-old boy with 8 weeks of a swollen right knee and a limp stiff each morning, easing by midday no diarrhea, urethritis or rash beforehand Lives in a city; no tick bites T 37.2 °C · ESR 28 mm/h → Juvenile idiopathic arthritis → arthritis for 6 weeks or more with morning stiffness and no other cause; a slit-lamp eye exam screens for uveitis
  7. 8-year-old boy with 5 days of painful joints and a limp left knee, then right ankle, then left elbow, one after another sore throat 3 weeks ago, untreated New soft apical murmur T 38.4 °C · ESR 60 mm/h → Acute rheumatic fever → migratory large-joint arthritis 2 to 4 weeks after pharyngitis: check an ASO titer and apply the Jones criteria; the murmur is carditis
  8. 5-year-old boy with 3 weeks of a limp leg pain that wakes him at night tired; bruises easily pale; lost weight this month T 37.8 °C · hip and knee motion full → CBC with smear → a limp with night pain, bruising, fatigue or weight loss: CBC with smear for leukemia before calling anything benign
  9. 14-year-old boy with 3 months of anterior knee pain worse with running and jumping in basketball tender, prominent tibial tubercle hip motion full and painless Afebrile · no night pain or weight loss → Osgood-Schlatter disease → the hip is cleared and the tibial tubercle is tender in an active adolescent: activity modification and NSAIDs
How NBME framed it: question 1

Healthy 16-month-old girl with a painless right-sided limp since she began walking 4 months ago term; cesarean delivery for breech presentation no family history of musculoskeletal disorders left leg shorter than the right left hip abduction limited to 30 degrees; right hip normal Sensation, circulation and strength normal

Most likely underlying mechanism?

Competing answers
  • Acute epiphyseal fracture: a toddler's limp; but it needs trauma, with pain, bruising and guarding; this limp is painless and 4 months old.
  • Acute suppurative arthritis: limited hip motion; but it brings fever and pain; she is healthy and painless.
  • Avulsion of muscle origin: a limp; but it follows an injury and hurts, often with a defect or mass.
  • Displacement of the capital femoral epiphysis: limited hip motion and a limp; but that is the adolescent slip, which limits internal rotation.
  • Failure of osteoid to mineralize: a toddler's leg problem; but rickets bows both legs; it does not shorten one or limit one hip.

Down to two: poorly developed acetabulum or displacement of the capital femoral epiphysis. Poorly developed acetabulum: a breech girl with a painless limp from her first steps, a short leg and limited abduction has DDH missed in infancy. Every option was a disease written as its mechanism. (The stem puts the limp on the right and the signs on the left; carried as written.)

Pairs with Septic Arthritis in a Child: the hot hip. Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis: the adolescent. Benign Limb Pain in a Child: the gait is normal. Suspected Child Abuse: Fractures and the Next Step: corner and femur fractures in a child who cannot walk; could he have generated the force? Congenital Muscular Torticollis and Plagiocephaly: a breech baby also needs a hip exam.
Transferable rule

Ask sick or well, then how old, then how long; a limp with night pain is a blood count first.
briefs.scfe:
Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis: Keep Off It and Pin It

Lost internal rotation at the growth spurt, whatever the build

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Stop weight bearing now (crutches or a wheelchair) and refer for urgent in situ screw fixation. Never force a reduction.

Suspect it at 10 to 15 years with hip, thigh or knee pain and a limp:

  • Internal rotation lost
  • The hip rotates outward on passive flexion
  • Knee pain with a normal knee exam

Obesity raises the risk but is not required: tall, thin adolescents slip during the growth spurt too.

Image both hips: AP (anteroposterior) and frog-leg lateral, or cross-table lateral if it may be unstable.

Atypical (under 8 or over 15, underweight, or short): look for an endocrine cause (hypothyroidism, GH (growth hormone) deficiency, panhypopituitarism, hypogonadism) or renal osteodystrophy.

Diagnosis
Defining findings Age – 10 to 15, the growth spurt; girls slip earlier than boys · Exam – lost internal rotation; obligate external rotation on passive flexion · Film – Klein line along the top of the femoral neck misses the epiphysis, or a widened, irregular physis · Slip – the epiphysis moves posteriorly and inferiorly through the hypertrophic zone
Two decoys Recent cold – the age and a weeks-long course rule out transient synovitis · Minor fall – it prompts the visit or tips a chronic slip into an unstable one; the slip came first. A femoral neck fracture needs high-energy trauma
Management and treatment
Management ladder: a slipped epiphysis
TierInterventionEscalate when
TodayNon-weight-bearing: crutches or a wheelchair; urgent orthopedic referralSlip confirmed on films
SurgeryIn situ fixation across the physis; never force a reductionNew groin pain or a narrowing joint space after fixation
ComplicationImage for osteonecrosis or chondrolysisTop rung
Around the fixation Other hip – bilateral in 20 to 40%; image it even when painless · Prophylactic pinning – considered for high risk: obesity, male sex, a first slip under age 10, an endocrine disorder · Does not stop the slip – bracing, casting, traction or physical therapy · Late – avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head, chondrolysis, early osteoarthritis
Practice
  1. 14-year-old boy with 4 weeks of intermittent left groin pain tripped on a stair this morning; now cannot bear weight at all, even with crutches left leg lies externally rotated Afebrile · radiograph: left femoral epiphysis displaced posteriorly → Unstable slipped capital femoral epiphysis → unable to bear weight even with crutches defines an unstable slip: osteonecrosis risk up to about half; keep him off it and pin urgently, without reduction
  2. 9-year-old girl was diagnosed today with a left slipped capital femoral epiphysis below the 5th percentile for height and the 10th for weight growth slowed over the past 2 years Fatigue and constipation HR 62/min · BP 100/64 mm Hg → Screen for hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, panhypopituitarism, renal osteodystrophy → short and underweight is atypical at any age: look for an endocrine or renal cause alongside fixation
  3. 12-year-old boy was diagnosed with a left slipped capital femoral epiphysis today pinning is scheduled right hip: no pain, full internal rotation Body mass index above the 95th percentile Afebrile · radiographs were taken of the left hip only → Radiographs of the right hip now → both hips are imaged at diagnosis: 20 to 40% of slips are bilateral, often silent at first
  4. 13-year-old boy with 3 weeks of aching right knee pain and a limp knee: no effusion, no tenderness, full painless motion ligament tests normal Plays football; no specific injury Afebrile · knee radiographs normal → Examine the hip → a normal knee exam sends you to the hip: a slip refers pain to the knee through the obturator nerve
  5. 14-year-old girl 5 months after screw fixation of a slipped left capital femoral epiphysis new left groin pain and stiffness hip motion now limited in all directions Afebrile · radiograph: narrowed joint space; screw position unchanged → Chondrolysis or AVN → joint space narrowing after fixation is cartilage loss (chondrolysis) or collapse of the head (osteonecrosis); an unchanged screw argues against hardware failure
  6. 16-year-old girl, a cross-country runner, with 3 weeks of right groin pain worse with each run; now hurts to hop on the right leg recently doubled her weekly mileage Afebrile · radiographs of both hips normal → Femoral neck stress fracture → groin pain on hopping with normal films after a training increase: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) for a femoral neck stress fracture
  7. 12-year-old girl with 3 weeks of right thigh pain since a minor fall today she cannot bear weight on the right leg right leg held externally rotated Afebrile · radiograph: right femoral epiphysis displaced off the neck → Forceful closed reduction of the slip → forcing the epiphysis back raises the risk of osteonecrosis: keep her off the leg and pin it where it lies
How NBME framed it: question 1

Previously healthy 13-year-old boy with 4 weeks of intermittent left groin pain and a limp no fever; not in acute distress height 50th percentile, weight 97th, body mass index above the 97th left hip: internal rotation and abduction limited; rotation to 75 degrees hurts; externally rotates on passive flexion Right hip and both knees normal T 37 °C · pulse 90/min · RR 20/min · BP 116/75 mm Hg AP and cross-table lateral films: irregular widening of the left femoral physis; mild osteopenia of the left femoral head and neck

Analgesia and weight-loss counseling given; next step?

Competing answers
  • Physical therapy: weeks of pain and stiffness; but it treats a strain after an injury, and there was none.
  • Abduction bracing: limited abduction; but it treats DDH (developmental dysplasia of the hip) in infants.
  • Traction: a painful hip and a limp; but it pulls a fractured bone to length; there was no trauma.
  • Spica cast immobilization: holding the hip still; but it holds an infant hip reduced for DDH.

Down to two: internal fixation or spica cast immobilization. Internal fixation: groin pain, lost internal rotation and a widened, irregular physis are a slip even before the epiphysis visibly moves; every other option treats another hip problem.

Pairs with The Limping Child: age and time for every limp. The Post-Traumatic Limb Mass: the adolescent thigh mass that dates to an injury.
Transferable rule

A stereotype is a prior, not a rule: when the exam fits and the patient does not, trust the exam and ask why.
